items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "herbicide"?
options: A large area of land on which only one type of crop is grown.
The build-up of a persistent substance, such as a pesticide, in organisms at higher trophic levels of a food chain.
items.answer: A pesticide that kills weeds.
items.markingKey: Herbicide: a pesticide that kills weeds.

items.stem: Explain why monocultures are more likely to suffer pest outbreaks.
items.answer: A large area of one crop provides abundant food for its pests, which can spread easily from plant to plant; predators have fewer habitats.

items.stem: Explain how intensive livestock production increases the efficiency of meat production.
items.answer: Animals are kept warm and their movement is restricted, so less energy is used in respiration for heat and movement; more goes into growth.
items.markingKey: less movement / heat loss [1]; more energy to growth [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2. Number of fronds, trial 1: 14, 30, 41, 29, 59; trial 2: 14, 30, 38, 49, 58; trial 3: 14, 31, 41, 51, 60. Calculate the mean number of fronds at 1 g/dm³, ignoring any anomalous result.

Noah grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. Number of fronds, trial 1: 21, 40, 52, 56, 61; trial 2: 14, 43, 51, 58, 60; trial 3: 14, 42, 51, 59, 63. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 0 g/dm³ (21 ); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Count the fronds in several beakers at each concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 at 0 g/dm³ identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: count the fronds in several beakers at each concentration; measure the dry mass of the duckweed instead of counting fronds; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the concentration of fertiliser (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Kenji grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Number of fronds, trial 1: 15, 53, 63, 69, 70; trial 2: 13, 55, 63, 67, 72; trial 3: 14, 53, 65, 95, 71. (a) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in the number of fronds from 0 g/dm³ to the highest concentration.
items.answer: (a) A line graph: concentration of fertiliser on the x-axis and mean number of fronds on the y-axis. (b) 407%
items.markingKey: (a) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; concentration of fertiliser on x-axis and number of fronds on y-axis [1] [2] (b) (71 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100 [1] = 407% [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is a negative impact of monocultures?
items.answer: Reduced biodiversity
items.markingKey: Removing other plants and animals reduces the variety of species.

items.stem: Explain how using pesticides on crops can harm organisms that are not pests.
items.answer: They may kill beneficial insects such as pollinators and predators; persistent pesticides bioaccumulate along food chains and harm top predators.

items.stem: The concentration of DDT (parts per million) was measured in a food chain near Kathmandu: soil water: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴; earthworms: 0.0442; thrushes: 0.486; sparrowhawks: 4.38. (a) Calculate how many times greater the concentration is in the sparrowhawks than in the earthworms. (b) Explain why the concentration increases along the food chain. (c) Suggest why the sparrowhawks may be harmed even though the concentration in the water is very low.
items.answer: (a) 99.1 times (b) DDT is persistent (not broken down or excreted); each organism eats many from the level below, so it accumulates (bioaccumulation). (c) It reaches toxic concentrations in top predators, e.g. thin eggshells or poisoning.
items.markingKey: (a) 4.38 ÷ 0.0442 [1] = 99.1 [1] (b) not broken down / excreted [1]; many prey eaten [1] (c) toxic dose [1] [5]

Number of fronds, trial 1: 14, 38, 51, 55, 60; trial 2: 13, 40, 48, 56, 58; trial 3: 19, 38, 50, 55, 55. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) Calculate the percentage increase in the number of fronds from 0 g/dm³ to the highest concentration.
items.answer: (a) Independent: concentration of fertiliser; dependent: number of fronds. (b) Count the fronds in several beakers at each concentration. (c) 327%

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the number of different species that live in an area"?
items.answer: Biodiversity
items.markingKey: Biodiversity: the number of different species that live in an area.

items.stem: Explain how deforestation can lead to extinction of species.
items.answer: Habitats and food sources are destroyed; species that live only in the forest cannot survive or reproduce.

items.stem: Explain how deforestation can change the local water cycle.
items.answer: Less transpiration means less water vapour enters the air, so less rainfall; soil becomes drier.

items.stem: Satellite images show the forest area in Sumatra fell from 5400 thousand km² in 1995 to 4855 thousand km² in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Calculate the mean rate of loss per year. (c) Assuming this rate continues, calculate how many more years it would take for all the forest to be lost. (d) State two consequences of this deforestation.
items.answer: (a) 10.1% (b) 27.25 thousand km² per year (c) 178 years (d) loss of habitats / extinction; soil erosion; flooding; increased CO₂.

items.stem: Satellite images show the forest area in the Amazon basin fell from 120 thousand km² in 1995 to 94 thousand km² in 2020. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Calculate the mean rate of loss per year. (c) Assuming this rate continues, calculate how many more years it would take for all the forest to be lost. (d) State two consequences of this deforestation.
items.answer: (a) 21.7% (b) 1.04 thousand km² per year (c) 90 years (d) loss of habitats / extinction; soil erosion; flooding; increased CO₂.

items.stem: In a region of tropical rainforest, large areas are being cleared for cattle ranching. Scientists report fewer species in the remaining forest, more frequent floods, and a fall in local rainfall. (a) Explain why there are fewer species in the remaining forest. (b) Explain why local rainfall has fallen.
items.answer: (a) Habitat loss and fragmentation; food webs disrupted; small isolated populations cannot find mates. (b) Fewer trees means less transpiration, so less water vapour enters the atmosphere to form clouds.

items.stem: Explain why soil in a deforested area becomes less fertile.
items.answer: Without roots, rain washes away topsoil (erosion) and mineral ions are leached; there is no leaf litter for decomposers to recycle nutrients.
items.markingKey: erosion [1]; leaching / no recycling [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why habitat destruction reduces biodiversity even in nearby areas.
items.answer: Remaining habitats become fragmented, so populations are small and isolated, food webs are disrupted, and species may be unable to find mates.

items.stem: Two plots on a hillside near Lagos received the same rainfall. Plot A was forested; plot B had been cleared. Water run-off: A 10.5%, B 56.6% of rainfall. Soil lost: A 0.4 tonnes per hectare, B 8.9 tonnes per hectare per year. (a) Calculate how many times more soil was lost from plot B. (b) Explain the difference in run-off. (c) Explain why the soil lost from B could cause flooding further downstream.
items.answer: (a) 22.2 times (b) In A, roots and leaf litter hold water and soil; trees take up and transpire water; B has no roots so water runs off. (c) Soil washes into rivers, raising the river bed so it overflows more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) 8.9 ÷ 0.4 = 22.2 [1] (b) roots hold soil / absorb water [1]; transpiration / interception [1] (c) silt in rivers [1] [4]

items.stem: In a region of tropical rainforest, large areas are being cleared for cattle ranching. Scientists report fewer species in the remaining forest, more frequent floods, and a fall in local rainfall. (a) Explain why there are fewer species in the remaining forest. (b) Explain how clearing the forest contributes to climate change.
items.answer: (a) Habitat loss and fragmentation; food webs disrupted; small isolated populations cannot find mates. (b) Less photosynthesis removing CO₂; burning and decay of trees release CO₂, an enhanced greenhouse effect.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "enhanced greenhouse effect"?
options: The process in which excess nutrients in water cause rapid growth of algae and, eventually, a fall in dissolved oxygen.
The release of substances into the environment that harm living organisms.
A rapid growth of algae in water rich in nutrients.
The increase in the greenhouse effect caused by extra greenhouse gases from human activities, leading to climate change.
items.answer: The increase in the greenhouse effect caused by extra greenhouse gases from human activities, leading to climate change.
items.markingKey: Enhanced greenhouse effect: the increase in the greenhouse effect caused by extra greenhouse gases from human activities, leading to climate change.

items.stem: Explain how untreated sewage can lead to the death of fish in a river.
items.answer: Sewage provides nutrients and organic matter; bacteria feed on it and multiply, respiring aerobically and using up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.
items.markingKey: bacteria decompose sewage [1]; aerobic respiration uses oxygen [1]; fish die [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how increased greenhouse gases lead to global warming.
items.answer: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared (heat) radiation emitted from the Earth's surface and re-radiate it, so less heat escapes to space and the temperature rises.

items.stem: In eutrophication, what happens immediately after this stage: "fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water"?
options: Algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die
Decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply
Fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen
items.answer: Algae grow rapidly (algal bloom)
items.markingKey: Sequence: fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water → algae grow rapidly (algal bloom) → algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die → decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply → the bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen → fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen.

items.stem: The stages of eutrophication are listed in the wrong order: A algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die; B fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen; C the bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen; D decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply; E fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water; F algae grow rapidly (algal bloom). Put the letters in the correct order.
items.answer: E → F → A → D → C → B
items.markingKey: E F A D C B: all correct [3]; four or five in correct positions [2]; two or three [1] [3]

items.stem: The stages of eutrophication are listed in the wrong order: A decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply; B fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen; C fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water; D algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die; E the bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen; F algae grow rapidly (algal bloom). Put the letters in the correct order.
items.answer: C → F → D → A → E → B
items.markingKey: C F D A E B: all correct [3]; four or five in correct positions [2]; two or three [1] [3]

items.stem: Yusuf measured dissolved oxygen in a river at different distances downstream from a sewage outlet, taking three samples at each site. Results table. Distance downstream / m: 0, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800. Dissolved oxygen concentration / mg/dm³, trial 1: 7.1, 2, 2.9, 3.4, 7.4, 9.6; trial 2: 6.8, 3.5, 2.9, 3.5, 7.5, 9.3; trial 3: 7.1, 3.3, 3, 3.6, 7.6, 9.5. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Explain why the oxygen concentration falls further on warm days.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 50 m (2 mg/dm³); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria respire faster.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 at 50 m identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) [2]

Distance downstream / m: 0, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. items.stem: Which term is defined as "the process in which excess nutrients in water cause rapid growth of algae and, eventually, a fall in dissolved oxygen"?
items.answer: Eutrophication
items.markingKey: Eutrophication: the process in which excess nutrients in water cause rapid growth of algae and, eventually, a fall in dissolved oxygen.

items.stem: In eutrophication, what directly causes the fall in dissolved oxygen?
options: Respiration of decomposer bacteria feeding on dead plants
items.answer: Respiration of decomposer bacteria feeding on dead plants
items.markingKey: Aerobic bacteria use up the oxygen.

items.stem: In eutrophication, what happens immediately after this stage: "algae grow rapidly (algal bloom)"?
options: Fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water
Algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die
Decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply
The bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen
items.answer: Algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die
items.markingKey: Sequence: fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) leaches into the water → algae grow rapidly (algal bloom) → algae cover the surface and block light, so plants below die → decomposers (aerobic bacteria) feed on the dead plants and multiply → the bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen → fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen.

items.stem: Ethan measured dissolved oxygen in a river at different distances downstream from a sewage outlet, taking three samples at each site. Results table. Distance downstream / m: 0, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. items.answer: (a) The dissolved oxygen falls just below the outlet to a minimum of about 3.3 mg/dm³ at 100 m, then rises again further downstream. (b) Take samples upstream of the outlet — shows the normal oxygen concentration without sewage. (c) Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria respire faster.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "the protection of species, habitats and resources from damage or loss"?
items.answer: Conservation
items.markingKey: Conservation: the protection of species, habitats and resources from damage or loss.

items.stem: Explain how captive breeding programmes can help conserve endangered species.
items.answer: Animals are bred in zoos, increasing numbers; individuals are chosen to maintain genetic variation; they can be released into protected habitats.

items.stem: Explain why fish stocks can collapse if fishing is not controlled.
items.answer: Fish are caught faster than they can reproduce; too few adults are left to breed, so the population cannot recover.

items.stem: The population of tigers in India was 5000 in 1990, 3371 in 2000 and 5108 in 2013, after a conservation programme began in 2000. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease between 1990 and 2000. (b) Calculate the percentage increase between 2000 and 2013. (c) Suggest two causes of the decline. (d) Suggest two measures that may have caused the increase.
items.answer: (a) 32.6% (b) 51.5% (c) habitat loss, poaching, conflict with farmers (d) protected reserves, anti-poaching patrols, captive breeding, education, legal protection.

items.stem: The population of orangutans in Borneo was 2400 in 2005, 1093 in 2013 and 1636 in 2023, after a conservation programme began in 2013. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease between 2005 and 2013. (b) Calculate the percentage increase between 2013 and 2023. (c) Suggest two causes of the decline. (d) Suggest two measures that may have caused the increase.
items.answer: (a) 54.5% (b) 49.7% (c) habitat loss, poaching, conflict with farmers (d) protected reserves, anti-poaching patrols, captive breeding, education, legal protection.

items.stem: Fewer than 100 individuals of the Amur leopard remain in the wild. A conservation group in Riyadh is planning how to save the species. (a) Suggest two other conservation measures. (b) Give two reasons why conservation of species is important.
items.answer: (a) Protect and restore habitat; anti-poaching laws and patrols; education; monitoring; reducing pollution. (b) Maintain biodiversity and food webs; possible medicines; ecosystem services; ethical / cultural reasons.

items.stem: Explain why artificial insemination and IVF are used in conservation.
items.answer: They allow breeding between individuals in different places, increasing genetic variation without transporting animals.

items.stem: Explain the importance of seed banks.
items.answer: They store seeds of many species and varieties, conserving genetic variation for future breeding or reintroduction if species become extinct in the wild.

items.stem: The breeding stock of cod in a fishing area (thousand tonnes): 2000: 1004, 2005: 860, 2010: 707, 2015: 617, 2020: 532. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease from 2000 to 2020. (b) A quota allows 20% of the 2020 stock to be caught. Calculate the mass that may be caught. (c) Describe two other methods of making fishing sustainable.
items.answer: (a) 47% (b) 106.4 thousand tonnes (c) larger mesh nets; closed seasons in breeding periods; protected areas; restocking from fish farms; education.

items.stem: Fewer than 80 individuals of the Philippine eagle remain in the wild. A conservation group in Seoul is planning how to save the species. (a) Explain why a very small population is at risk of extinction even if it is protected. (b) Describe how a captive breeding programme could help.
items.answer: (a) Low genetic variation (inbreeding), so a disease or environmental change could kill all of them; few mates. (b) Breed in captivity to increase numbers; choose mates to maximise genetic variation (use studbooks, artificial insemination, IVF); release into protected habitat.

items.stem: Why do farmers add nitrate fertilisers to crops?
options: To provide nitrogen for making amino acids and proteins
items.answer: To provide nitrogen for making amino acids and proteins
items.markingKey: Nitrate is needed for protein synthesis and growth.

items.stem: Explain why using antibiotics routinely in intensive livestock farming is a concern.
items.answer: It selects for antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which may spread to humans.

items.stem: A farm in Doha grows maize on 50 hectares. Without fertiliser the yield was 2.5 tonnes per hectare; with fertiliser it was 3.4 tonnes per hectare. (a) Calculate the extra mass of maize produced on the whole farm. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in yield. (c) State one environmental risk of using too much fertiliser.
items.answer: (a) 45 tonnes (b) 36% (c) fertiliser washes (leaches) into rivers and lakes, causing eutrophication.

items.stem: The concentration of DDT (parts per million) was measured in a food chain near Muscat: water: 2.0 × 10⁻⁵; algae: 0.0170; water fleas: 0.239; small fish: 1.43; herons: 12.9. (a) Calculate how many times greater the concentration is in the herons than in the algae. (b) Explain why the concentration increases along the food chain. (c) Suggest why the herons may be harmed even though the concentration in the water is very low.
items.answer: (a) 759 times (b) DDT is persistent (not broken down or excreted); each organism eats many from the level below, so it accumulates (bioaccumulation). (c) It reaches toxic concentrations in top predators, e.g. thin eggshells or poisoning.
items.markingKey: (a) 12.9 ÷ 0.0170 [1] = 759 [1] (b) not broken down / excreted [1]; many prey eaten [1] (c) toxic dose [1] [5]

items.stem: Isla grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. Number of fronds, trial 1: 8, 42, 53, 56, 60; trial 2: 15, 41, 54, 55, 59; trial 3: 14, 41, 53, 60, 59. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) As the concentration of fertiliser increases, the number of fronds increases and then levels off at about 1.5 g/dm³. (b) Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins for growth, so more fronds are produced; at high concentrations another factor (e.g. light, space) becomes limiting, so the increase levels off.

items.stem: Which is a reason for habitat destruction?
options: Clearing land for farming and housing
items.answer: Clearing land for farming and housing

items.answer: (a) 15.4% (b) 55.53 thousand km² per year (c) 82 years (d) loss of habitats / extinction; soil erosion; flooding; increased CO₂.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term algal bloom.
items.answer: A rapid growth of algae in water rich in nutrients.

items.stem: Explain why discarded plastic can harm seabirds.
items.answer: Birds mistake plastic for food; it fills the stomach so they starve, or they become entangled.

items.stem: Explain why eutrophication is more likely after heavy rain on recently fertilised fields.
items.answer: Rain dissolves soluble fertiliser and washes (leaches) it into rivers and lakes.

items.stem: Estimated times to break down in the environment: fishing line 600 years; banana peel 0.1 years. (a) Explain why some items take hundreds of years to break down. items.stem: After heavy rain on farmland near a lake in Auckland, the water turned green. Two weeks later the water became clear and brown, and many dead fish were seen. (a) Explain why the water turned green. (b) Suggest two ways farmers could reduce this problem.
items.answer: (a) Fertiliser (nitrate / phosphate) washed into the lake; algae grew rapidly (algal bloom). (b) Use less fertiliser or organic fertiliser; avoid spreading before heavy rain; leave buffer strips of vegetation near water.

items.stem: Explain how resources such as forests and fish stocks can be managed sustainably, and describe the role of seed banks and captive breeding in conservation.
items.answer: Forests: replanting, selective felling, education, laws. Fish: quotas, net mesh size, closed seasons, protected areas, restocking. Seed banks preserve genetic variation of plants; captive breeding, AI and IVF increase numbers and variation of endangered animals for release.

items.stem: Which is a disadvantage of intensive livestock production?

items.answer: Disease spreads easily between crowded animals

items.stem: Diego grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Number of fronds, trial 1: 14, 49, 59, 59, 61; trial 2: 14, 49, 54, 61, 59; trial 3: 13, 46, 58, 58, 64. (a) Calculate the mean number of fronds at 2 g/dm³. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in the number of fronds from 0 g/dm³ to the highest concentration.

Ines grew duckweed in beakers of mineral solution containing different concentrations of nitrate fertiliser and counted the number of fronds after 14 days. Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Results table. Concentration of fertiliser / g/dm³: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2. Number of fronds, trial 1: 14, 33, 44, 80, 66; trial 2: 14, 31, 42, 53, 61; trial 3: 14, 31, 42, 56, 64. items.answer: (a) Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins for growth, so more fronds are produced; at high concentrations another factor (e.g. light, space) becomes limiting, so the increase levels off. items.answer: (a) 22.9% (b) 7.45 thousand km² per year (c) 67 years (d) loss of habitats / extinction; soil erosion; flooding; increased CO₂.

items.stem: Two plots on a hillside near Manila received the same rainfall. Plot A was forested; plot B had been cleared. Water run-off: A 11.9%, B 36.5% of rainfall. Soil lost: A 0.3 tonnes per hectare, B 9.8 tonnes per hectare per year. (a) Calculate how many times more soil was lost from plot B. (b) Explain the difference in run-off. (c) Explain why the soil lost from B could cause flooding further downstream.
items.answer: (a) 32.7 times (b) In A, roots and leaf litter hold water and soil; trees take up and transpire water; B has no roots so water runs off. (c) Soil washes into rivers, raising the river bed so it overflows more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) 9.8 ÷ 0.3 = 32.7 [1] (b) roots hold soil / absorb water [1]; transpiration / interception [1] (c) silt in rivers [1] [4]

items.stem: Fewer than 80 individuals of the Sumatran rhino remain in the wild. A conservation group in Santiago is planning how to save the species. (a) Suggest two reasons why the species became endangered. (b) Explain why a very small population is at risk of extinction even if it is protected. (c) Give two reasons why conservation of species is important.
items.answer: (a) Habitat destruction; hunting / poaching; pollution; introduced species; climate change. (b) Low genetic variation (inbreeding), so a disease or environmental change could kill all of them; few mates. (c) Maintain biodiversity and food webs; possible medicines; ecosystem services; ethical / cultural reasons.
